drills.los_text: discuss the role of, and a framework for, capital market expectations in the portfolio management process
drills.reading_name: Capital Market Expectations, Part 1: Framework and Macro Considerations

questions.stem: In setting capital market expectations, the most important objective is most likely:

options.A: matching historical average returns for each asset class.
options.B: forecasting each asset class return precisely.
options.C: maintaining consistency across asset classes and horizons.

rationales.A: Extrapolating long-run historical averages was the standard practice before the 1990s, and it is identified as a flawed model rather than an objective. It contributed directly to the misallocation seen at the height of the technology bubble, when past returns were projected forward indefinitely. Matching a historical average is a method, and a discredited one, not the goal the process is meant to serve.
rationales.B: Undue emphasis on the precision of individual asset class projections is explicitly warned against. Even sophisticated methods produce large forecast errors, so precision for any single asset class cannot be the governing objective. A set of individually precise but mutually inconsistent inputs still produces a portfolio with poor risk-return characteristics, which is why precision ranks below consistency.
rationales.C: Internal consistency is described as a far more important objective than the precision of individual projections. It has two dimensions: cross-sectional consistency, meaning the expectations for different asset classes hang together at a point in time, and intertemporal consistency, meaning the expectations for different horizons hang together over time. Inconsistent inputs are exploited by the optimizer, which loads up on whichever asset class the inconsistency happens to flatter, producing portfolios with poor risk-return characteristics.

questions.stem: An analyst is preparing a CME report and, at designated times, synthesizes her ongoing market monitoring, documents her views, and defends them to the investment committee. Within the seven-step CME framework, this activity most likely corresponds to:

options.A: Step 6 (document the conclusions).
options.B: Step 2 (research the historical record).
options.C: Step 5 (interpret the current environment).

rationales.A: Step 6 is, at designated times, to synthesize, document, and defend one's views. That is exactly the activity described: the formal provision of the expectations set, together with documented reasoning, presented to and defended before the investment committee. The defining feature is that it happens at designated points in the cycle rather than continuously.
rationales.B: Step 2 is researching the historical record: studying past return behavior and identifying the drivers behind it. It is background work that precedes a forecast, and it is not the synthesis and delivery of current views to a committee.
rationales.C: Step 5 is implementing the investment and research process, the day-to-day work of monitoring conditions and interpreting the current investment environment. It is contrasted explicitly with Step 6: Step 5 is continuous, while the activity described here is the designated-time synthesis that follows it.

questions.stem: A good capital market forecast is most likely:

options.A: unbiased, efficient, and internally consistent.
options.B: long-horizon, model-driven, and readily revised.
options.C: precise, timely, and quantitative.

rationales.A: Good forecasts have three properties. They are unbiased, objective, and well researched, so no systematic distortion is built in. They are efficient, in the sense of minimizing forecast errors. And they are internally consistent, both cross-sectionally across asset classes and intertemporally across horizons.
rationales.B: Horizon length, model form, and revisability are not among the three named properties. A forecast can be long-horizon, built from a model, and routinely revised, and still be biased, inefficient, and internally inconsistent, so none of the three attributes guarantees forecast quality.
rationales.C: Precision is explicitly downplayed: large forecast errors are unavoidable even with sophisticated methods, and internal consistency matters more than the accuracy of any single projection. Timeliness and quantification are not among the three named properties either, useful as they may be in practice.

questions.stem: An analyst uses a discounted cash flow model to forecast long-term equity returns and a business-cycle-based model to forecast short-term returns. To satisfy intertemporal consistency, the short-term model is most likely required to:

options.A: converge to the long-range forecast as the horizon extends.
options.B: be re-estimated whenever the long-range forecast is updated.
options.C: produce forecasts below the long-range forecast.

rationales.A: Where one method is used for long-horizon projections and another for short-horizon projections, intertemporal consistency dictates that the method used for the short-horizon projections be calibrated so that its projections converge to the long-range forecast as the horizon extends. Without that calibration the two models imply two different long-run equilibria, and the expectations set contradicts itself across horizons.
rationales.B: Re-estimating the short-term model whenever the long-range forecast is updated is not what intertemporal consistency requires. A model can be re-estimated on every update and still settle on a different long-run value than the discounted cash flow model does. Convergence, not the frequency of re-estimation, is the requirement.
rationales.C: There is no directional requirement. A business-cycle-based model may place short-horizon expected returns above or below the long-run forecast depending on where the economy sits in the cycle, and a model forced permanently below the long-run forecast would itself violate consistency. Only convergence as the horizon lengthens is required.

questions.stem: In the first step of the capital market expectations framework, specifying the expectations needed, the asset class universe should most likely be:

options.A: as broad as the major capitalization-weighted indices.
options.B: as large as possible.
options.C: as small as the firm's distinct allocations permit.

rationales.A: Letting index composition set the universe ignores the firm's own investment process. The universe should reflect the asset classes that will actually be accorded distinct allocations in client portfolios, which is a decision about how the firm invests rather than about how an index provider weights a benchmark.
rationales.B: Expanding the universe beyond what the investment process needs is counterproductive. The expectations-setting process can be quite challenging even at minimum scope, and each asset class added brings with it another mean, another variance, and a full row of covariances to estimate, all of which must remain internally consistent.
rationales.C: The universe should include all asset classes that will typically be accorded a distinct allocation in client portfolios, but should otherwise be as small as possible, because the expectations-setting process can be quite challenging even at that minimum scope. Coverage is set by the firm's allocation decisions; beyond that point, smaller is better.

questions.stem: In setting capital market expectations, the appropriate frequency of the return data used is most likely:

options.A: daily for short horizons and annual for long horizons.
options.B: daily for short horizons and daily for long horizons.
options.C: annual for short horizons and annual for long horizons.

rationales.A: Appropriate data frequencies must be selected to match the forecast horizon. Daily series are of more use in setting shorter-term expectations, while monthly, quarterly, or annual series are useful for setting longer-term capital market expectations. The frequency follows the horizon being forecast rather than being fixed in advance.
rationales.B: Daily data is not preferred at every horizon merely because it supplies more observations. Frequency is matched to horizon, and daily and weekly data carry a specific cost: asynchronism becomes a significant problem at those frequencies, particularly across markets in different time zones, which distorts measured covariances and correlations.
rationales.C: Annual-only data is not the recommendation. Higher-frequency series have a legitimate role in shorter-horizon work, where additional observations improve the precision of variance and covariance estimates; discarding them in favor of annual data alone throws away that precision.

questions.stem: Even with a well-designed capital market expectations process, real-time quantitative evaluation of forecast errors is most likely:

options.A: a better guide to process flaws than qualitative judgment.
options.B: a formality once a few forecast cycles have passed.
options.C: a weaker guide to process flaws than qualitative judgment.

rationales.A: Quantitative error evaluation cannot outrank qualitative judgment as a guide to where the process went wrong, because the observations needed to support it are not there. A standard rule of thumb is that at least 30 observations are needed to test a hypothesis meaningfully, and that threshold is rarely reached in practice for forecast evaluation.
rationales.B: The evaluation does not shrink to a formality as cycles accumulate. The sample grows only slowly, because the capital market expectations cycle is typically annual, so reaching even 30 observations takes decades rather than a few cycles.
rationales.C: A standard rule of thumb is that at least 30 observations are needed to test a hypothesis meaningfully, and with a typically annual expectations cycle that sample accumulates very slowly. As a result, quantitative evaluation of forecast errors is of limited value in refining a reasonably well-constructed process, and the most valuable part of the feedback loop will often be qualitative and judgmental: reviewing whether the reasoning behind a forecast held up, not whether the number did.

questions.stem: The shift by institutional investors from extrapolating historical returns to explicitly forward-looking methods most likely occurred because:

options.A: regulators mandated forward-looking projections.
options.B: modern databases made historical returns easier to compute.
options.C: bubble-era extrapolation produced unrealistic projections.

rationales.A: Regulation is not identified as the driver of the shift. Institutions moved toward forward-looking methods in response to what the experience of the bubble revealed about extrapolation, not in response to a mandate requiring them to do so.
rationales.B: The ease of computing historical returns from modern databases is not the cited driver. If anything, cheaper and faster access to historical return series would have entrenched the historical-extrapolation approach rather than displaced it; what changed was confidence in the method, not the cost of applying it.
rationales.C: At the height of the technology bubble, extrapolating historical return data led many investors to project double-digit portfolio returns into the indefinite future. Those projections allowed institutions to underfund obligations and to set unrealistic goals, since the assumed returns appeared to do the work that contributions otherwise would. Since then, most institutions have adopted explicitly forward-looking methods, and projected returns have declined sharply.

questions.stem: An analyst estimating a covariance matrix for a global multi-asset portfolio is considering a move from monthly to daily return observations. Higher-frequency data is most likely to:

options.A: improve the precision of variances and covariances, but not of means.
options.B: improve the precision of means and variances, but not of correlations.
options.C: improve the precision of the sample means, but not of the variances.

rationales.A: Higher-frequency data improves the precision of sample variances, covariances, and correlations, because those estimates benefit from the sheer number of observations. It does not improve the precision of the sample mean, which is governed by the length of the sample period rather than by how finely that period is sliced. Raising the frequency carries a separate cost, asynchronism: at daily and weekly frequencies, markets in different time zones trade at non-overlapping times, so a common-dated return series mismeasures how markets actually move together, and that problem grows as frequency rises.
rationales.B: The claim fails on both halves. Correlation precision does improve with higher-frequency data, alongside variances and covariances, so excluding correlations is wrong. And mean precision does not improve, because the sample mean depends on the sample horizon rather than the observation frequency, so including means is wrong as well.
rationales.C: This reverses the relationship. Higher-frequency data does not improve the precision of the sample mean, which is governed by the length of the sample period, while it does improve the precision of variances, covariances, and correlations. Observing a fixed span more finely adds information about dispersion and co-movement, not about the average rate of drift over that span.

questions.stem: A study finds that US bond returns from 1980 through 2008 exhibited a strong negative correlation with inflation, but the same relationship did not hold over the subsequent 2009-2021 period. This is most likely a consequence of:

options.A: The peso problem.
options.B: Survivorship bias.
options.C: Nonstationarity.

rationales.A: The peso problem describes ex-post returns that understate ex-ante risk because a feared adverse event never materialized within the sample period. It concerns a tail outcome missing from the data, not a relationship that holds over one span of years and then fails over the next.
rationales.B: Survivorship bias arises when failed entities drop out of a data set, leaving only the survivors and so overstating performance and understating risk. It is notorious in hedge fund data. It does not account for a correlation between bond returns and inflation that reverses between adjacent periods, since the bond market itself did not drop out of the sample.
rationales.C: Nonstationarity means that different parts of a data series reflect different underlying statistical properties as a result of changes in regime. The relationship between bond returns and inflation is the standard illustration: the span described covers at least three distinct monetary policy and inflation regimes, so the strong negative correlation estimated through 2008 carries no assurance of holding thereafter. The practical consequence is that the usable sample is limited to the current regime, which is precisely the tension with the desire for long data histories.

questions.stem: During a period when the market rallied sharply, an analyst's clients pressured her to increase allocations to the outperforming asset. She justified the increase by pointing to strong recent earnings growth, having previously lost clients by doubting a prior similar rally. The biases she is most likely exhibiting include:

options.A: Availability and confirmation biases.
options.B: Anchoring and prudence biases.
options.C: Overconfidence and time-period biases.

rationales.A: Being strongly influenced by a memorable past experience — having lost clients by doubting an earlier rally — is availability bias: the forecast is driven by how easily that outcome comes to mind rather than by its true likelihood. Reaching for the evidence that supports the conclusion the clients already want, here strong recent earnings growth, is confirmation bias: evidence on valuation or on whether that earnings growth can persist is not sought with equal effort. The two biases reinforce each other, which is why the justification arrives after the allocation decision rather than before it.
rationales.B: Anchoring bias is placing excessive weight on an initial value or forecast and then adjusting it too little as new information arrives. Prudence bias is tempering a forecast toward the consensus so as not to appear extreme, which would push the analyst away from raising the allocation rather than toward it. Neither describes an analyst reacting to a vivid memory and then assembling support for a conclusion she has already reached.
rationales.C: Overconfidence bias is unwarranted confidence in one's own judgment, typically showing up as forecast ranges that are too narrow; here the analyst is deferring to client pressure and to her own recollection rather than over-trusting her own analysis. Time-period bias is a data and sampling problem — a sample window too short to be representative, or long enough to span structural change — not a psychological bias of the forecaster.

questions.stem: An analyst reviewing a colleague's report notes that the report treats returns as if drawn from a normal distribution and uses long-term historical averages to estimate expected market returns even in the current low-yield environment. The most serious issue with this approach is most likely:

options.A: Model uncertainty.
options.B: Parameter uncertainty.
options.C: Input uncertainty.

rationales.A: Model uncertainty is the risk that the model itself is wrong, and it is potentially the most serious of the three because the wrong model leads to fundamentally flawed conclusions rather than merely imprecise ones. Treating returns as drawn from a stable normal distribution, and then estimating expected returns from long-run historical averages regardless of the current low level of yields, is a structural assumption about how markets work, not an estimation detail. The same flawed framework misled institutional investors in the run-up to the tech bubble. No amount of additional data or more careful estimation repairs a forecast built on a model that does not describe the world.
rationales.B: Parameter uncertainty is estimation error in a model's coefficients: the structure is accepted and the inputs are the right ones, but the estimates are imprecise. It is mitigated by due attention to estimation error — standard errors, longer or cleaner samples, shrinkage toward a prior. That is a second-order concern when the distributional assumption underlying the whole report may be wrong.
rationales.C: Input uncertainty arises when a variable the model requires cannot be observed and a proxy must be substituted, the classic case being the market portfolio in the CAPM. The report's problem is not the measurement of an unobservable input but the assumption of normally distributed returns estimated from historical averages.

questions.stem: In 2002, the Argentine peso, previously pegged 1:1 to the US dollar, devalued sharply to 3.8 ARS/USD after a decade of stable exchange rates. An analyst studying the pre-2002 sample of returns on Argentine assets denominated in pesos is most likely to:

options.A: Underestimate ex ante risk and overestimate expected return.
options.B: Estimate both ex ante risk and expected return without bias.
options.C: Overestimate ex ante risk and underestimate expected return.

rationales.A: This is the peso problem: ex ante prices during the sample period already reflected the possibility of a very negative event — abandonment of the peg — that did not materialize within the sample. Looking backward at that decade, realized volatility is low because the feared event never happened, so ex ante risk is underestimated; realized returns are high because investors were being paid a premium for bearing a risk that never arrived, so ex ante expected returns are overestimated. A decade of stable 1:1 rates followed by devaluation to 3.8 ARS/USD is the textbook illustration, and the lesson generalizes to any regime held together by a policy commitment that may be abandoned.
rationales.B: Estimates drawn from the peg period are biased, not unbiased. A sample in which a priced, feared outcome stays dormant systematically understates risk and overstates return, because the compensation for bearing that risk is collected inside the sample while the loss it compensates for falls outside it.
rationales.C: Both directions run the other way. Currency risk being priced into peso asset yields is precisely what lifts realized returns while realized volatility stays low, so an ex post estimate taken from the peg period understates ex ante risk rather than overstating it. The same premium, collected inside the sample for a devaluation that fell outside it, makes the sample overstate rather than understate ex ante expected return.

questions.curriculum_ref: Ex Post Risk Can Be a Biased Measure of Ex Ante Risk — Argentine peso

questions.stem: An analyst tests hundreds of technical indicators against historical returns and identifies one with a statistically significant relationship. The most appropriate safeguard against data-mining bias in this finding is to:

options.A: Construct an economic explanation for the relationship once found.
options.B: Require an explicit economic rationale and test out of sample.
options.C: Extend the sample period until the relationship is confirmed.

rationales.A: Constructing an explanation after the relationship has been discovered is the practice the safeguard is meant to defeat, not the safeguard itself. A plausible story can be found for almost any result turned up by searching hundreds of candidates, and publishing on that basis passes the data-mining bias on to the reader.
rationales.B: The guidance is to scrutinize the variable selection process for signs of data mining, to require an explicit economic rationale for why the variable should have forecasting power — 'no story, no future' — and to examine the forecasting relationship out of sample, on data not used to estimate it. The rationale has to come from economics rather than from the search, and the out-of-sample test is what separates a real relationship from one of the many significant-looking results that appear by chance when hundreds of indicators are screened at a 5% significance level.
rationales.C: Extending the sample period until the relationship is confirmed is another pass of the same search, run over sample periods instead of indicators, and it compounds the data-mining problem rather than controlling it. Additional data help only when the window is fixed in advance and used to test the relationship, not to confirm it.

questions.stem: A hedge-fund index shows realized volatility of 6% and correlation with equities of 0.15, based on monthly self-reported returns from funds that value certain positions via appraisal. Compared with true underlying volatility and correlation, the reported figures are most likely:

options.A: Volatility biased downward and correlation understated.
options.B: Volatility biased upward and correlation overstated.
options.C: Volatility and correlation both unbiased.

rationales.A: Appraised, or smoothed, values move less than market-determined prices because an appraisal partly carries the prior valuation forward instead of marking fully to current information. Measured volatility is therefore biased downward — the reported 6% understates the volatility of the underlying positions — and measured correlation with liquid markets such as equities is understated as well, because a smoothed series responds to common shocks with a lag rather than contemporaneously. A reported correlation of 0.15 thus overstates the diversification actually on offer. The effect applies to hedge funds holding appraisal-valued positions just as it does to real estate, and monthly self-reporting adds a selection element on top of the smoothing.
rationales.B: Smoothing dampens reported movements, so both figures are biased downward, not upward. Were the bias upward, appraisal-based series would appear more volatile and more correlated than the markets their holdings are drawn from, which is the opposite of what is observed.
rationales.C: The bias is real, systematic and one-directional. Taking the reported 6% volatility and 0.15 correlation at face value produces an allocation built on more diversification and less risk than the positions actually carry.

questions.curriculum_ref: Data Measurement Errors and Biases — appraisal (smoothed) data

questions.stem: An analyst's dataset for computing daily 5% VaR on a single stock contains 22 observations from March 2020. Two of the 22 observations were declines exceeding 9% (on March 12 and March 16). Using this sample to project 5% VaR going forward is most likely to:

options.A: Produce an accurate estimate of tail risk.
options.B: Overstate the likelihood of large future losses.
options.C: Understate the likelihood of large future losses.

rationales.A: A rare event over-represented in a short window does not make the sample realistic; it makes the sample systematically biased upward for tail risk. Twenty-two daily observations cannot pin down the frequency of an event that occurs a handful of times in a decade, and March 2020 is the least representative month available.
rationales.B: This is the mirror image of the peso problem. Within a finite sample the observed frequency of a rare bad outcome can far exceed its true probability: two declines of more than 9% in 22 trading days implies such losses roughly 9% of the time, a frequency no plausible return distribution supports over the long run. A 5% VaR projected from that window therefore substantially overstates both the likelihood and the size of similarly large future losses. In the case this example is drawn from, the stock recorded no comparable single-day loss over the following 19 months. The remedy is a sample long enough to contain a representative number of stress episodes, or an explicit model of the tails rather than raw historical frequencies.
rationales.C: The finite-sample problem here is over-representation of the rare event, not under-representation. Two observations are indeed few, but they are two extreme observations out of 22, which pushes the estimated frequency of large losses up rather than down.

questions.curriculum_ref: Ex Post Risk Can Be a Biased Measure of Ex Ante Risk — VaR overstate

drills.los_text: explain how exogenous shocks may affect economic growth trends
drills.reading_name: Capital Market Expectations, Part 1: Framework and Macro Considerations

questions.stem: A primary source of exogenous shocks to a country's trend rate of economic growth is least likely to be:

options.A: Weaker consumer confidence.
options.B: Discovery of new natural resources.
options.C: Geopolitical conflict that diverts resources.

rationales.A: A swing in consumer confidence is a business cycle phenomenon — a fluctuation around the trend — rather than an exogenous shock that shifts the trend itself. The six categories identified as shock sources are policy changes, new products and technologies, geopolitics, natural disasters, natural resources and critical inputs, and financial crises. Confidence appears on none of them: it is a channel through which shocks and cycles transmit, not a source of shocks.
rationales.B: Discovery of new natural resources, or of new ways to recover known ones, is named as a shock category, with hydraulic fracturing as the standard example: it raised potential output by lowering the cost of a critical input.
rationales.C: Geopolitics is explicitly a shock category, and it cuts both ways — the fall of the Berlin Wall as a positive example, and conflicts or defense buildups that divert resources to less productive uses as negative ones.

questions.stem: Following a severe financial crisis, an economy's output falls sharply and does not recover to its pre-crisis level; however, its subsequent growth rate returns to the pre-crisis trend. This crisis is most likely classified as:

options.A: A Type 1 crisis.
options.B: A Type 2 crisis.
options.C: A Type 3 crisis.

rationales.A: A Type 1 crisis is a persistent, one-time decline in the level of output with the subsequent trend rate of growth unchanged. That is exactly the pattern described: output is permanently lower, but the economy then grows from the lower base at the old rate, so the shortfall against the pre-crisis path stays constant instead of widening.
rationales.B: A Type 2 crisis shows no persistent decline in the level of output but a reduced subsequent trend rate of growth — output regains its old path and then grows more slowly, so the shortfall widens over time. That is the reverse of the pattern described.
rationales.C: A Type 3 crisis combines both effects: a persistent decline in the level of output and a reduction in the subsequent trend rate of growth. Here only the level decline occurs, since growth returns to its pre-crisis trend.

questions.curriculum_ref: Section 3 — Example 6, three types of crises

questions.stem: Trend changes in economic growth that arise from truly exogenous shocks are best described as:

options.A: Readily identifiable from immediate traces in the data.
options.B: Built into asset prices in advance of the change itself.
options.C: Unforeseeable and hard to quantify until well established.

rationales.A: The opposite holds. Changes of this kind are difficult to identify, assess and quantify until they are well established and retrospectively revealed in the data; the traces are neither immediate nor obvious, which is why such trend breaks are usually recognized late.
rationales.B: The effect of a truly exogenous shock will not have been built into asset prices in advance, precisely because the event was not foreseeable. The general risk that shocks of this kind occur may well be priced, but the specific trend change is not, and that distinction is what makes exogenous shocks consequential when expectations are set.
rationales.C: Trend changes driven by truly exogenous shocks are not only impossible to foresee but also difficult to identify, assess and quantify until the change is well established and retrospectively revealed in the data. The practical consequence for capital market expectations is that the analyst must form a judgment about the shock's persistence long before the data can confirm a new trend, while avoiding the opposite error of reading an ordinary cyclical move as a trend break.

questions.stem: A country enacts a major, permanent overhaul of its business tax code, sharply lowering corporate rates while streamlining regulation. The most likely effect on trend economic growth is:

options.A: No effect on trend growth.
options.B: A downward shift in trend growth.
options.C: An upward shift in trend growth.

rationales.A: Policy changes are one of the primary sources of trend-shifting exogenous shocks. A permanent cut in corporate tax rates alters private-sector incentives to invest, hire and locate activity, so it acts on potential output rather than merely transferring income; treating taxation as a neutral transfer ignores that incentive channel entirely.
rationales.B: Pro-growth tax reform is characterized as growth-enhancing, the 2017 US Tax Cuts and Jobs Act being the standard illustration. Lower revenue could in principle crowd out public investment, but a permanent reduction in corporate rates combined with streamlined regulation is classified as raising the expected trend rate of growth, not lowering it.
rationales.C: Sound tax policy and a light regulatory burden are elements of pro-growth government policy, and any significant, unexpected change in these policies that is likely to persist will change the expected trend rate of growth. A permanent cut in corporate rates alongside streamlined regulation raises the after-tax return on investment and lowers compliance costs, both of which support a larger capital stock and higher productivity, so the expected trend rate shifts upward. The 2017 US business tax overhaul is the example commonly cited as an intended change of this kind.

questions.stem: The eurozone experienced a sharp decline in output after the 2007–2009 global financial crisis and did not recover to its pre-crisis trend growth rate. This experience most likely represents a financial crisis featuring:

options.A: A persistent level decline and reduced trend growth.
options.B: Reduced trend growth with no persistent level decline.
options.C: A persistent level decline with unchanged trend growth.

rationales.A: This combination — a persistent decline in the level of output together with a reduction in the trend growth rate — is the Type 3 crisis, and the eurozone is the standard illustration of it. Output fell sharply and never returned to the pre-crisis trend path, and the trend growth rate itself stepped down. The usual attribution is structural: rigid labor markets, an aging population and the absence of fiscal integration, compounded by policy missteps such as a slow monetary policy response and insolvent banks left operating rather than resolved.
rationales.B: Reduced trend growth with no persistent decline in the level of output is the Type 2 crisis. It does not fit here because the eurozone did suffer a sharp and persistent drop in the level of output, which is given in the facts.
rationales.C: A persistent level decline with an unchanged trend growth rate is the Type 1 crisis: output settles onto a lower path but grows at the old rate thereafter. It does not fit here because the eurozone never recovered its pre-crisis trend growth rate, so the trend itself changed.

questions.stem: The fall of the Berlin Wall triggered German reunification and a 'peace dividend' as governments cut defense spending. This event is most likely classified as a:

options.A: Growth-enhancing domestic fiscal reform.
options.B: Growth-diminishing geopolitical shock.
options.C: Growth-enhancing geopolitical shock.

rationales.A: The defense cuts were a consequence of a geopolitical event — the end of the Cold War — rather than a domestic fiscal reform. The episode is presented as an exogenous geopolitical shock to growth, so this answer gets the direction of the effect right but misidentifies its source.
rationales.B: The event was indeed geopolitical, but it is classified as growth-enhancing rather than growth-diminishing: the 'peace dividend' released resources previously devoted to defense for more productive uses. Reunification costs and cutbacks at defense contractors were real, but they do not make the net effect on growth negative in this treatment.
rationales.C: The fall of the Berlin Wall and the subsequent 'peace dividend' is the standard example of a growth-enhancing geopolitical shock: resources tied up in defense were freed for productive use across the affected economies. Geopolitics is not one-directional — tensions such as the space race can themselves spur innovation that yields growth-enhancing technologies — so the sign of a geopolitical shock has to be judged case by case rather than assumed negative.

questions.stem: A major hurricane destroys productive capacity in a coastal region. Treating the disaster as an exogenous shock, the most likely effect on growth is:

options.A: Lower growth in the short run and possibly higher growth in the long run.
options.B: A permanent increase in trend growth as rebuilding proceeds.
options.C: A permanent reduction in both the level of output and trend growth.

rationales.A: Natural disasters destroy productive capacity, so in the short run a disaster is likely to reduce growth. Over the long run growth may actually be enhanced, because the capacity that was destroyed can be replaced with newer and more efficient facilities. The short-run and long-run effects therefore carry opposite signs, which is why a disaster cannot simply be entered into a forecast as a negative.
rationales.B: Rebuilding lifts measured activity only temporarily, and the immediate effect of destroyed capacity is lower growth, not a boost. Any long-run improvement comes from old capacity being replaced with more efficient facilities, not from rebuilding expenditure permanently raising the trend rate of GDP growth.
rationales.C: A permanent reduction in both the level of output and the trend growth rate, with no recovery mechanism, overstates the damage. The replacement of destroyed capacity with more efficient facilities is a recognized channel through which long-run growth can end up higher, not lower.

questions.stem: In the decomposition of trend GDP growth into labor inputs and labor productivity, the labor productivity component most likely consists of:

options.A: Capital deepening plus growth in total factor productivity.
options.B: Potential labor force growth plus growth in participation.
options.C: Growth in hours worked plus growth in real wages.

rationales.A: Trend growth splits into growth from labor inputs and growth from labor productivity. The labor productivity half is growth from increasing capital inputs — capital deepening, meaning more capital per worker — plus growth in total factor productivity, which captures technological progress and other efficiency gains that are not attributable to using more capital or more labor.
rationales.B: Growth in the size of the potential labor force plus growth in the labor force participation rate is the labor inputs component of trend growth, not the labor productivity component. Both halves are needed to build up trend growth, but this answer names the wrong one.
rationales.C: Neither term belongs in the labor productivity split. Hours worked is an element of labor input rather than of output per unit of input, and real wages describe how income is distributed between labor and capital rather than any source of productivity growth.

questions.stem: An analyst projects long-run US equity returns from trend growth. She estimates labor input growth of 0.7%, labor productivity growth of 1.5%, inflation of 2.0%, and a dividend yield of 1.8%. Assuming no further growth in the P/E multiple, her baseline projection for continuously compounded long-term equity returns is closest to:

rationales.A: This is roughly the nominal trend growth figure on its own — labor input growth plus labor productivity growth plus inflation, 0.7% + 1.5% + 2.0% = 4.2% — with the 1.8% dividend yield omitted. The dividend yield has to be added because the investor earns income in addition to the capital appreciation that tracks nominal growth in aggregate equity value.
rationales.B: A figure of this size requires either double-counting one of the components or adding a term for expansion of the P/E multiple. The analyst has explicitly ruled out the repricing term by assuming no further growth in the multiple, so there is nothing to add beyond growth, inflation and income.
rationales.C: Baseline projection = labor input growth + labor productivity growth + inflation + dividend yield = 0.7% + 1.5% + 2.0% + 1.8% = 6.0%. The first two terms sum to real trend growth of 2.2%; adding inflation gives nominal trend growth of 4.2%, which is the anchor for growth in the aggregate value of equity; the 1.8% dividend yield is then added as the income component of total return. Because the multiple is assumed flat, no term for a change in the P/E is included.

questions.stem: The empirical evidence on economic growth and equity markets across countries most likely indicates that countries with higher economic growth rates:

options.A: Do not reliably generate higher equity returns.
options.B: Reliably generate higher equity returns.
options.C: Generate higher equity returns only when the growth is anticipated.

rationales.A: Studies covering a wide cross-section of markets — Klement (2015), for instance, spans 44 countries — find that countries with higher economic growth rates do not reliably generate higher equity market returns. Two partial explanations are usually offered: expected higher growth may already be reflected in share prices, so investors pay for it in advance and earn no excess return from it; and rapid growth in the capital stock can drive down the rate of return on invested capital, so faster aggregate growth does not translate into faster per-share earnings growth.
rationales.B: The evidence runs the other way. A reliable link from national growth rates to equity market returns is exactly what the cross-country studies fail to find, which is why a growth forecast on its own is a weak basis for allocating between national equity markets.
rationales.C: Anticipation appears in this literature as one partial explanation for why high growth does not produce high returns — growth already in the price earns nothing extra — not as a condition under which the relationship does hold. Reversing it into a condition gets the role of the argument backwards: if anything, only unanticipated growth could help, and the studies establish no reliable link either way.

questions.curriculum_ref: Section 4 — growth and equity returns discussion

questions.stem: The trend rate of growth provides an important anchor for estimating long-run bond returns. This is most likely because:

options.A: Inflation is procyclical and averages to zero over the cycle.
options.B: Central banks target policy rates equal to the trend growth rate.
options.C: Average real default-free yields are linked to real trend growth.

rationales.A: Inflation is indeed procyclical, but it does not average to zero over the cycle; under a credible inflation-targeting regime it averages to the central bank's target. The anchoring argument runs through the level of real yields and real trend growth, not through inflation washing out of the nominal yield.
rationales.B: Central banks do not set policy rates equal to the trend growth rate. They target inflation and, in some frameworks, an output gap, and the policy rate is a short-term instrument. The anchor for long-run bond returns comes instead from the level toward which yields are pulled over long horizons.
rationales.C: Both theory and empirical evidence indicate that the average level of real — and correspondingly nominal — default-free bond yields is linked to the trend rate of real (nominal) growth. Yields fluctuate around that level and are drawn back toward it over time, so an estimate of trend growth pins down the average yield a long-horizon bond investor can expect to earn, which is what makes trend growth an anchor for bond return expectations.

questions.curriculum_ref: Section 4 — anchoring asset returns to trend growth

questions.stem: The aggregate market value of equity in an economy is most likely expressed as the product of:

options.A: Trend growth, the equity risk premium and the dividend yield.
options.B: Book value, return on equity and the P/E multiple.
options.C: GDP, capital's share of income and the P/E multiple.

rationales.A: Trend growth, the equity risk premium and the dividend yield are inputs to an expected return, not multiplicative components of the level of aggregate equity value. Multiplying them together produces no meaningful quantity.
rationales.B: Book value multiplied by return on equity gives earnings, and the P/E multiple capitalizes those earnings, so this is a valuation identity at the level of an individual firm. It is not the aggregate market decomposition, which has to begin from the size of the economy rather than from a company's balance sheet.
rationales.C: Aggregate equity market value is expressed as V_e = GDP × S^k × P/E, where S^k is capital's share of income, that is, earnings divided by GDP. The decomposition matters because capital's share of income cannot rise or fall indefinitely, and neither can the P/E multiple. With both of those terms bounded over the long run, the growth rate of the total value of equity in an economy is tied to the growth rate of GDP, which is why trend growth anchors long-run equity return expectations.

questions.curriculum_ref: Anchoring Asset Returns to Trend Growth — equity identity

questions.stem: Which of the following is least likely a use of trend growth analysis in setting capital market expectations?

options.A: A discipline on DCF earnings forecasts.
options.B: A predictor of short-term cyclical turning points.
options.C: An anchor for real government bond yields.

rationales.A: This is one of the identified uses. Earnings projections in a discounted cash flow valuation have to be kept consistent with aggregate long-run growth, since the companies in an economy cannot all grow faster than the economy indefinitely.
rationales.B: Trend growth is a long-horizon construct and is not a tool for calling short-term business cycle turning points or inflation spikes; that is the work of business cycle analysis, which is treated separately. The four uses of trend growth analysis are: imposing discipline on DCF earnings forecasts; identifying high-growth countries that may offer attractive equity returns provided the growth is not already reflected in prices; judging how fast actual growth can run before inflation becomes a concern, since a higher trend permits faster actual growth; and anchoring expectations for real government bond yields.
rationales.C: This is one of the identified uses. Faster trend real growth implies a higher average level of real default-free yields, so an estimate of trend growth anchors long-run government bond return expectations.

questions.curriculum_ref: Applying Growth Analysis to Capital Market Expectations — four uses

questions.stem: Over their development path, emerging market economies most likely experience trend growth that is:

options.A: Rapid during catch-up and slower as they become more developed.
options.B: Persistently slower than in developed markets.
options.C: Constant and in line with global averages.

rationales.A: Most countries have gone through periods of both faster and slower trend growth over the course of their development. Emerging economies often grow rapidly while catching up with the leading industrial countries, as they adopt existing technology and deepen a thin capital stock, but the more developed they become, the more likely it is that their growth will slow toward the pace of the leaders. A forecast therefore cannot simply extend the catch-up growth rate indefinitely.
rationales.B: This reverses the catch-up pattern. Emerging market trend growth is typically faster than developed market growth during the catch-up phase, and only converges downward as development proceeds.
rationales.C: Trend growth is not constant over a country's development path, which is why a single historical average makes a poor forecast. Emerging economies in particular tend to grow faster than global averages while catching up and then decelerate.
