drills.los_text: compare major approaches to economic forecasting
drills.reading_name: Capital Market Expectations, Part 1: Framework and Macro Considerations

questions.stem: An analyst wants the simplest forecasting approach that still provides useful information about upcoming changes in economic activity, inflation, interest rates, and security prices. The most appropriate approach is:

options.A: Checklists.
options.B: Leading indicators.
options.C: Econometric models.

rationales.A: Checklists are straightforward but time-consuming, because they require continually monitoring the widest possible range of data. They are the most flexible of the three approaches, since any question the analyst thinks relevant can be added, but flexibility is not simplicity: the breadth of data to be tracked grows rather than shrinks.
rationales.B: Leading indicator-based analysis is the simplest forecasting approach to use, because it requires following only a limited number of statistics. It also requires no assumptions about the paths of exogenous variables, and the indicators are selected precisely because their turns precede turns in economic activity, inflation, interest rates, and security prices.
rationales.C: Econometric models are complex and time-consuming to formulate, and the data inputs they require are themselves not easy to forecast. They impose discipline and consistency on the analysis and quantify the effect of exogenous variables, but on the dimension asked about here they are the opposite of simple.

questions.stem: A key weakness of the leading indicator approach to economic forecasting is most likely:

options.A: Inability to quantify the impact of exogenous variables.
options.B: Subjectivity based on the forecaster's judgment.
options.C: Frequent revisions to the indicator history.

rationales.A: Not requiring forecasts or quantitative impact estimates of exogenous variables is a strength of the indicator approach, not a weakness. Indicators are built to signal upcoming turns without the forecaster having to model the exogenous drivers behind them, which is part of why the approach is the simplest of the three. The recognized weaknesses are false signals and the look-ahead bias embedded in the indicator history.
rationales.B: Subjectivity and reliance on the forecaster's judgment are weaknesses of the checklist approach, where the analyst subjectively integrates the answers to a self-selected list of questions. The leading indicator approach is quantitative and rule-based: the component series and their weights are set in advance, so discretion in assembling the signal is not where its problems come from.
rationales.C: The composite indicator's entire history may be revised each month as components are redefined, reweighted, or restated. That makes the current published series unreliable as an input for historical analysis and leaves the index overfitted in sample: the series as published today tracks past turning points better than the series actually available in real time ever did, so backtests flatter the approach. That is the look-ahead bias, and it sits alongside the approach's other weakness, false signals.

questions.stem: A strength of econometric modeling in economic forecasting is most likely:

options.A: Forecasting turning points well.
options.B: Adapting quickly to structural change.
options.C: Imposing discipline and consistency on analysis.

rationales.A: Rarely forecasting turning points well is a listed weakness of econometric models, not a strength. The relationships in the model are estimated as averages over the sample period, so the model tends to extrapolate the prevailing regime straight through the point at which it breaks.
rationales.B: Econometric models assume the historical relationships among variables are stable. When the structure of the economy changes, a model estimated on past data can remain misspecified for an extended period, because re-estimation needs enough post-change observations to identify the new relationships. Handling structural change is therefore a weakness of the approach, not a strength.
rationales.C: Imposing discipline and consistency on the analysis is the recognized strength of econometric modeling: the model forces every forecast to respect the same explicit relationships and the same accounting identities, and it produces quantitative estimates of the impact of exogenous variables. Its matching weaknesses are that it is complex and time-consuming to formulate, that its inputs are hard to forecast, and that it rarely forecasts turning points well.

questions.stem: Nowcasting is most likely aimed at:

options.A: Forecasting GDP two years ahead.
options.B: Predicting turning points in the yield curve.
options.C: Forecasting GDP for the current quarter.

rationales.A: Nowcasting is not designed to be predictive of anything beyond the end of the current quarter. Its purpose is to fill the reporting gap before the first official estimate of output arrives, so a projection two years out is the work of a structural econometric model, not of a nowcast.
rationales.B: Nowcasting targets GDP itself, not yield curve dynamics. It reads incoming activity data as they are released and makes no claim about where the term structure turns or when an inversion signal arrives.
rationales.C: Nowcasting forecasts GDP for the current quarter, which will not be released until after quarter-end, based on data as they are released throughout the quarter. The best-known example is the Atlanta Fed's GDPNow, which is in effect a running forecast of the Bureau of Economic Analysis's advance estimate and is updated as each new monthly release arrives.

questions.stem: The three distinct approaches to economic forecasting are most likely:

options.A: Structural, technical, and behavioral.
options.B: Econometric models, indicators, and checklists.
options.C: Top-down, bottom-up, and hybrid.

rationales.A: These are not the three recognized approaches to economic forecasting. Structural and behavioral describe classes of model or sources of investor behavior rather than forecasting frameworks, and technical analysis works on market prices rather than on the economy.
rationales.B: The three approaches are econometric models, the most formal and mathematical, built on explicit relationships estimated from historical data; indicators, variables that lead, lag, or move coincidentally with turns in the economy; and checklists, the subjective integration of the answers to a set of relevant questions. Thorough analysis typically incorporates elements of all three, because each approach's weaknesses are covered by another's strengths.
rationales.C: Top-down and bottom-up describe the direction in which an analysis is assembled, and hybrid simply combines them. They classify how security and portfolio analysis is organized, not the approaches used to forecast the economy.

questions.stem: The OECD composite leading economic indicator (LEI) for each country or region is most likely based on:

options.A: Monthly GDP releases.
options.B: A single manufacturing indicator.
options.C: Five to nine cyclical variables.

rationales.A: GDP is released quarterly, not monthly, and it is the variable the leading indicator is built to anticipate rather than an input to it. The composite is assembled instead from cyclical series such as share prices, manufacturing metrics, inflation, interest rates, and monetary data, all of which are available well before the quarterly national accounts.
rationales.B: A composite leading indicator aggregates several series precisely so that the idiosyncratic noise in any one of them averages out. Relying on a single manufacturing series would forfeit that benefit and would leave the signal hostage to one sector's own cycle.
rationales.C: The OECD composite leading economic indicator for each country or region is based on five to nine variables, such as share prices, manufacturing metrics, inflation, interest rates, and monetary data, that exhibit cyclical fluctuations similar to those of GDP. Their peaks and troughs occur six to nine months before the corresponding peaks and troughs in GDP with reasonable consistency, and that lead is what makes the composite useful.

questions.stem: A composite measure of how many individual leading indicators are pointing up versus down is most likely called:

options.A: A nowcast.
options.B: An econometric consensus index.
options.C: A diffusion index.

rationales.A: Nowcasting is a separate technique that forecasts GDP for the current quarter from data released during it. It produces an estimate of the level of output, not a count of how many indicators are rising.
rationales.B: This is not a recognized term. A consensus index in ordinary usage aggregates forecasters' opinions rather than the directions of indicator series, and an econometric model yields a point forecast rather than a breadth count.
rationales.C: Individual leading indicators can be combined into a diffusion index, which measures how many of them are pointing up and how many down. If seven of ten are pointing upward, the odds are that the economy is accelerating. The index captures the breadth of the signal rather than its magnitude, so it can show a turn spreading across sectors before any single series moves decisively.

questions.stem: The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) releases a sequence of three GDP estimates for each quarter. In order, they are most likely:

options.A: Flash, preliminary, and revised.
options.B: Advance, preliminary, and final.
options.C: Estimate, benchmark, and audit.

rationales.A: Flash and revised are not the names used for these releases. The first of the three is the advance estimate and the third is the final estimate; only the middle release is correctly named here.
rationales.B: The Bureau of Economic Analysis releases three estimates of each quarter's GDP: the advance estimate, published about four weeks after quarter-end and carrying the greatest market impact because it is the first official reading; the preliminary estimate a month later; and the final estimate at the end of the following quarter. The Atlanta Fed's GDPNow is a forecast of the advance estimate, which is why its accuracy is judged against that release rather than against the final figure.
rationales.C: These are not the names of the three quarterly releases. Benchmark revisions are a separate and infrequent exercise that restates the national accounts over many years, and no quarterly GDP audit is published.

drills.los_text: discuss how business cycles affect short- and long-term expectations
drills.reading_name: Capital Market Expectations, Part 1: Framework and Macro Considerations

questions.stem: The business cycle is conventionally divided into five phases. In sequence starting from the trough, these are most likely:

options.A: Recovery, expansion, peak, contraction, trough.
options.B: Trough, recovery, expansion, peak, decline.
options.C: Initial recovery, early expansion, late expansion, slowdown, contraction.

rationales.A: This listing mixes phases with turning points: the peak and the trough are the turning points that bound the cycle, not phases within it. It corresponds to the simpler two-segment description of a cycle, which is not the classification used for setting capital market expectations.
rationales.B: The trough and the peak are turning points rather than phases, and decline is not one of the five phase names. The sequence also collapses early and late expansion into one phase, and that is the distinction that matters most for returns, because the two halves of an expansion carry very different inflation and policy risk.
rationales.C: The five phases are initial recovery, a short phase beginning at the trough; early expansion; late expansion; slowdown; and contraction. The first four all occur within the overall expansion, so the upswing is described through four distinct phases while the downswing is a single one, reflecting that expansions last longer and change character as they age.

questions.curriculum_ref: Section 6 — five phases of the business cycle

questions.stem: An economy's output gap has closed, unemployment is low, profits are strong, wages and inflation are rising, capacity pressures are boosting investment spending, and debt coverage ratios are deteriorating. The economy is most likely in:

options.A: Late expansion.
options.B: Early expansion.
options.C: Slowdown.

rationales.A: Late expansion is the phase in which the output gap has closed and the economy is increasingly in danger of overheating. A boom mentality prevails: unemployment is low, profits are strong, both wages and inflation are rising, and capacity pressures boost investment spending. Debt coverage ratios may deteriorate as borrowers lever against strong current earnings. That is the configuration described.
rationales.B: Early expansion still runs with a negative output gap that is closing. Profits are rising from a low base, but the labor market is not yet tight, inflation is typically still subdued, and spare capacity means capacity pressures are not what drives investment. The closed output gap and rising wages described here rule the phase out.
rationales.C: In a slowdown the output gap has begun to reopen: business confidence weakens, profit growth stalls, and firms raise prices to stay ahead of costs that are still climbing. The strong profits and boom conditions described belong to the phase before it, not to the slowdown.

questions.stem: Business cycle analysis is most likely to produce its most reliable signal for capital market expectations over a horizon of:

options.A: One to three years.
options.B: Less than three months.
options.C: Ten years or more.

rationales.A: The cyclical signal is likely to be most reliable, with a higher signal-to-noise ratio and hence most value to the forecaster, over horizons within the range of likely expansion and contraction phases — perhaps one to three years. Over that span the economy is plausibly still within the phase being analyzed, so the cyclical position maps onto realized returns.
rationales.B: Returns over substantially shorter horizons are likely to be driven primarily by market reactions to more transitory developments — news, flows, sentiment — which undermines the cycle's predictive value rather than sharpening it. The cyclical position barely moves over three months, while return noise is large.
rationales.C: Over very long horizons, one or more turning points will occur within the horizon, so realized returns reflect an average over the whole cycle. That averaging reduces the cycle's predictive value toward the 'information-less' long-run mean rather than increasing it.

questions.stem: A five-year equity return forecast is being prepared. Compared with the same forecaster's forecast for a three-month horizon starting today, business cycle position information is most likely:

options.A: Less heavily weighted.
options.B: Weighted the same.
options.C: More heavily weighted.

rationales.A: As the horizon lengthens, a forecast should put increasing weight on averaging over expansion and contraction phases and converge toward the 'information-less' long-term average return. A five-year horizon is likely to span one or more turning points, so today's cyclical position is diluted; a three-month horizon starting today sits inside the current phase, where that position carries its greatest weight.
rationales.B: The weight attached to cyclical position varies by horizon rather than being fixed by the model. The same starting point produces very different forecasts depending on how many cycle transitions the horizon is likely to span, so an unchanged model does not imply unchanged weighting.
rationales.C: This reverses the direction of the relationship. Longer horizons dilute, rather than amplify, the information in the current cyclical position, because the economy is expected to pass through other phases before the horizon ends.

questions.stem: In the initial recovery phase of the business cycle, capital market effects are most likely characterized by:

options.A: Sharply rising short-term rates, an inverted yield curve, and declining stocks.
options.B: Low short-term rates and bond yields, briskly rising stocks, and strong cyclical assets.
options.C: Peaking short-term rates, topping bond yields, and widening credit spreads.

rationales.A: These are the conditions of the slowdown phase, not of initial recovery. In a slowdown the central bank is still tightening or has just finished, short-term rates rise sharply, the yield curve may flatten or invert, and equities decline as earnings expectations are cut.
rationales.B: Initial recovery runs for a few months after the trough. Short-term rates and government bond yields are low, stimulative monetary and fiscal policies are still in place, the output gap is negative, and inflation is still decelerating. Bond yields may continue declining but are likely bottoming. Stock markets may rise briskly as recession fears dissipate. Cyclical assets — small-cap stocks, higher-yield corporate bonds, and emerging market equities and bonds — attract investors and typically perform well.
rationales.C: This also describes the slowdown phase: short-term rates are at or near their cyclical peak, bond yields are topping out, and credit spreads begin to widen as the outlook deteriorates. In initial recovery, rates and yields are near cyclical lows and spreads are narrowing from elevated levels.

questions.curriculum_ref: Phases of the Business Cycle — initial recovery

questions.stem: Across US business cycles since 1854, the average duration of contraction phases and of expansion phases, respectively, is closest to:

options.A: 5 months and 10 months.
options.B: 42 months and 17 months.
options.C: 17 months and 42 months.

rationales.A: These durations are far too short on both counts. The shortest complete US cycle on record ran 17 months peak to peak, so a 5-month average contraction plus a 10-month average expansion would imply a typical full cycle of about 15 months.
rationales.B: This reverses the two averages. Expansions have on average been much longer than contractions, not the other way around; a 42-month average contraction against a 17-month average expansion would describe an economy contracting most of the time.
rationales.C: The United States has experienced 34 complete business cycles since 1854, averaging 59 months from peak to peak. The longest ran 146 months and the shortest 17 months. On average, contraction phases (peak to trough) lasted 17 months and expansion phases (trough to peak) lasted 42 months, which sums to the 59-month average cycle.

questions.curriculum_ref: Business Cycle Peaks and Troughs — NBER stats

questions.stem: At a fundamental level, the business cycle most likely arises from:

options.A: A single well-defined periodic cycle of fixed length.
options.B: Purely random shocks with no cyclical structure.
options.C: The superposition of many cycles of differing frequencies.

rationales.A: The business cycle is not a specific, well-defined cycle with a fixed length. Historical cycles have varied substantially in both duration and intensity, which is inconsistent with a single periodic process; US cycles since 1854 have run from 17 to 146 months peak to peak.
rationales.B: The cycle has structure rather than being pure randomness. The underlying cycles are stochastic, but they are cycles: they generate the recurring expansion and contraction pattern that makes cyclical position informative for forecasting at all.
rationales.C: The business cycle is the result of many intermediate-frequency cycles, ranging from very short to very long, that jointly generate most of the variation in aggregate economic activity around the trend. This superposition explains why historical cycles have varied in both duration and intensity — each realized cycle is a different draw from a range of underlying stochastic cycles.

questions.stem: In the contraction phase of the business cycle, capital market effects most likely include:

options.A: Sharply rising short-term rates, rising bond yields, and a flattening curve.
options.B: Short-term rates and bond yields at cyclical peaks, with an unchanged yield curve.
options.C: Declining short-term rates and bond yields, with a sharply steepening curve.

rationales.A: This describes the late expansion or slowdown phases, when the central bank is tightening into an overheating economy: short-term rates rise sharply, bond yields rise, and the curve flattens or inverts. In contraction the policy direction has reversed.
rationales.B: Rates change substantially during a contraction rather than sitting still at their peaks. Rates and yields peak at the end of the slowdown phase; once contraction is under way, central bank easing pulls them down and the curve reshapes.
rationales.C: A contraction typically lasts 12 to 18 months. Central bank easing drives short-term rates down, bond yields fall, and the yield curve steepens substantially because the front end falls further than the long end. Stocks decline in the earlier stages but usually start to rise in the later stages, well before the recovery emerges. Credit spreads widen and remain elevated until signs of a trough appear.

questions.curriculum_ref: Phases of the Business Cycle — contraction

drills.los_text: explain the relationship of inflation to the business cycle and the implications of inflation for cash, bonds, equity, and real estate returns
drills.reading_name: Capital Market Expectations, Part 1: Framework and Macro Considerations

questions.stem: Under a credible central bank inflation target, the horizon structure of inflation expectations is most likely:

options.A: Countercyclical — upward sloping at the trough and inverted at the peak.
options.B: Acyclical — flat at both the trough and the peak.
options.C: Procyclical — steep at the peak and inverted at the trough.

rationales.A: The horizon structure of inflation expectations is countercyclical: upward sloping at the trough of the business cycle and inverted at the peak. Short-horizon expectations move with current inflation — low at the trough, high at the peak — while very long-horizon expectations stay anchored to the target, so the slope between them flips with the cycle.
rationales.B: Long-run expectations are virtually unaffected by cyclical fluctuations when the target is credible, which is why the far end is anchored. But short-horizon expectations have about the same amplitude as actual inflation, so the near end moves with the cycle and the term structure is not flat.
rationales.C: This reverses the direction of the pattern. At the peak, current and hence short-horizon inflation is high relative to the anchored long-run target, so the structure is inverted, not steep; at the trough it is upward sloping.

questions.curriculum_ref: Section 7 — horizon structure of inflation expectations

questions.stem: As long as inflation remains within its expected cyclical range, the effect on stocks and bonds is most likely:

options.A: Significant for stocks but limited for bonds.
options.B: Significant for bonds but limited for stocks.
options.C: Significant for both stocks and bonds.

rationales.A: This reverses the two sensitivities. Bonds are always affected because their nominal cash flows are fixed, so inflation feeds straight through to the discount rate with no offset. Stocks are relatively insensitive as long as inflation stays within its expected cyclical range.
rationales.B: For bonds, because cash flows are fixed in nominal terms, the effect of inflation is transmitted solely through the discount rates, so there is nothing to offset a change in expected inflation. For stocks, as long as inflation stays within the expected cyclical range, there should be little effect because both expected future cash flows and the associated discount rates rise or fall in line with the horizon structure of inflation expectations, and the two effects largely cancel.
rationales.C: Stocks are the asset class identified as having little effect from inflation within the expected cyclical range, because nominal cash flows and discount rates move together. Equities become inflation-sensitive only once inflation moves outside that range, in either direction.

questions.curriculum_ref: Section 7 — asset class effects of inflation

questions.stem: In a persistent deflationary environment, the effects across asset classes most likely include:

options.A: Unattractive cash, benefits for top-quality bonds, impairment of lower-quality debt.
options.B: Attractive cash at the zero bound, benefits for top-quality bonds, impairment of lower-quality debt.
options.C: Unattractive cash, losses for all bonds, benefits for equities.

rationales.A: Cash is not unattractive in deflation. Deflation may make cash particularly attractive if a zero lower bound is binding on the nominal interest rate, since a zero nominal return is a positive real return when prices are falling. The two bond claims here are correct, but the treatment of cash is not.
rationales.B: All three effects hold. Cash may be particularly attractive when the zero lower bound is binding, because a nominal return floored at zero still earns a positive real return while the price level falls. Persistent deflation benefits the highest-quality bonds because it increases the purchasing power of their fixed cash flows. And it is likely to impair the creditworthiness of lower-quality debt, because falling prices raise the real burden of the borrower's fixed obligations against shrinking nominal revenue.
rationales.C: Bonds are not uniformly hurt: the highest-quality bonds benefit, since their nominal cash flows are certain and gain purchasing power. Equities are typically hurt rather than helped, because deflation-driven weakness in nominal revenue and earnings outweighs any benefit from lower discount rates. Cash is also mischaracterized, for the reason given under the zero lower bound.

questions.stem: Real estate cash flows in the short-to-intermediate term are most likely dictated by:

options.A: Existing lease contracts.
options.B: The level of nominal interest rates.
options.C: Current inflation expectations.

rationales.A: Short- to intermediate-term nominal cash flows from real estate are generally dictated by existing leases, with the speed of adjustment depending on the type of real estate asset held. Lease renewal is the point at which inflation is passed through to rental income, so short-lease property types adjust quickly and long-lease property types behave much more like fixed-income claims over the near term.
rationales.B: Interest rates affect the discount rate applied to the property and the cost of any financing, but they do not reset the rental income already contracted under existing leases. The effect runs through valuation, not through near-term cash flows.
rationales.C: Inflation expectations matter for longer-term cash flow projections, once leases roll and rents can be repriced. They do not change the cash flows locked in by leases already in force over the short to intermediate term.

questions.stem: Cash, defined as short-term interest-bearing instruments, is best described as:

options.A: a high-duration nominal asset with substantial inflation risk.
options.B: a real-return hedge against equity market declines.
options.C: a zero-duration, inflation-protected asset earning a floating real rate.

rationales.A: Cash has near-zero duration, not high duration: the yield on short-term instruments resets continually, so principal value is almost insensitive to a move in rates. For the same reason its inflation risk is limited rather than substantial, because the nominal rate it earns adjusts with expected inflation.
rationales.B: Cash is not a hedge against equity market declines. Its protection operates directly through the relationship between short-term nominal rates and inflation, not through any reliable negative co-movement with equities.
rationales.C: As long as short-term interest rates adjust with expected inflation, cash is essentially a zero-duration, inflation-protected asset that earns a floating real rate. Inflation above or below expectation contributes to temporary fluctuations in the realized real return. Cash's real rate is procyclical around a long-term level consistent with the central bank's target inflation.

questions.stem: Most central banks implicitly or explicitly target a positive rate of inflation most likely because:

options.A: a small positive inflation rate maximizes seigniorage revenue.
options.B: positive inflation reliably widens corporate profit margins.
options.C: policy is better at restraining activity than at stimulating it, and deflation is damaging.

rationales.A: Seigniorage is not an objective of modern monetary policy. The positive-inflation buffer reflects asymmetric policy effectiveness and the desire to avoid deflation's damage to debt-financed investment and to the power of central banks, not revenue considerations.
rationales.B: Inflation that stays within its normal cyclical range is generally neutral for stocks at the aggregate level. Whether an individual firm's margins widen depends on its pass-through pricing power, so no reliable aggregate margin gain follows from positive inflation.
rationales.C: Two drivers are at work. First, asymmetric policy effectiveness: central bank tools are generally more effective in slowing activity than in accelerating sluggish activity, so banks tend to be more aggressive in resisting downward pressure on the economy than in reining in strong demand. This asymmetric reaction function argues for aiming above zero rather than at zero. Second, deflation damages debt-financed investment, because the real burden of existing debt rises, and it damages the power of central banks, because policy rates constrained near or below zero limit the stimulus available.

questions.curriculum_ref: Inflation and Deflation — asymmetric reaction function

questions.stem: Rising expected inflation that stays within the expected cyclical range would most likely cause nominal bond prices to:

options.A: rise.
options.B: remain unchanged.
options.C: fall.

rationales.A: This has the wrong sign. Coupons being fixed is what exposes the bond: with cash flows unable to grow, a higher discount rate can only reduce the present value, so rising expected inflation produces capital losses rather than gains.
rationales.B: Fixed nominal cash flows are precisely why the discount-rate channel matters rather than why it does not. Inflation cannot reach the numerator of a nominal bond, so all of its effect passes through the denominator, and prices respond.
rationales.C: Because bond cash flows are fixed in nominal terms, the effect of inflation is transmitted solely through discount rates. Rising inflation induces capital losses as the expected-inflation component of yields rises. If inflation stays within the expected cyclical range, shorter-term yields rise more than longer-term yields, but the shorter yields have less price impact because of their shorter duration.

questions.stem: Higher-than-expected inflation is most likely to cause property values and expected rental income to:

options.A: remain flat.
options.B: rise.
options.C: decline.

rationales.A: Leases do not lock in nominal rates permanently. As leases come up for renewal they progressively re-price to reflect prevailing inflation expectations, so real estate income is not insulated from an inflation surprise and values are not neutral to it.
rationales.B: Higher-than-expected inflation is likely to coincide with high demand for real estate, expectations that rental income will rise even faster than general inflation, and rising property values. However, the impact may be idiosyncratic, depending on lease length, existing supply, and the new-supply pipeline.
rationales.C: This has the wrong sign. Higher-than-expected inflation is associated with high demand for real estate, expectations that rental income will rise even faster than general inflation, and rising property values; the upward adjustment in rents is not overwhelmed by the rise in nominal discount rates.

drills.los_text: discuss the effects of monetary and fiscal policy on business cycles
drills.reading_name: Capital Market Expectations, Part 1: Framework and Macro Considerations

questions.stem: A central bank targets an inflation rate of 2.0%, with a neutral real policy rate of 2.25% and trend growth of 2.5%. If expected inflation is 3.0% and expected growth is 3.5%, the Taylor rule target nominal policy rate is closest to:

rationales.A: 3.25% is the real rate implied by the same Taylor rule calculation, that is, the target nominal rate less expected inflation (i* - pi-e = 6.25% - 3.0%). The question asks for the nominal policy rate, so expected inflation must be left in.
rationales.B: 5.25% would require omitting either the expected inflation term or one of the two gap terms from the rule. Dropping both half-gaps, for example, leaves 2.25% + 3.0% = 5.25%, but the output gap and the inflation gap are both positive here and each adds 0.5%.
rationales.C: The Taylor rule is i* = r_neutral + pi-e + 0.5 x (growth-e - growth-trend) + 0.5 x (pi-e - pi-target) = 2.25% + 3.0% + 0.5 x (3.5% - 2.5%) + 0.5 x (3.0% - 2.0%) = 2.25% + 3.0% + 0.5% + 0.5% = 6.25%. The economy is running above trend and inflation is running above target, so the rule calls for a policy rate above the sum of the neutral real rate and expected inflation.

questions.stem: The analogy that expansionary policy is like pushing on a string, whereas restrictive policy is like pulling on a string, most likely describes:

options.A: the yield curve response to quantitative easing versus tightening.
options.B: the political feasibility of easing versus tightening.
options.C: the asymmetric effectiveness of policy in slowing versus stimulating activity.

rationales.A: The analogy applies to conventional monetary policy in general, not specifically to balance sheet programs such as quantitative easing and tightening, and it is a statement about the transmission of policy to the real economy rather than about the shape of the yield curve.
rationales.B: The analogy is about how effective policy is once enacted, not about how easy it is to enact. Tightening is often the politically harder of the two, which is the opposite of what this reading of the analogy would imply.
rationales.C: The analogy describes the asymmetry that central banks' policy tools are more effective in slowing economic activity than in accelerating sluggish activity. Restrictive policy pulls the string and the economy follows; expansionary policy pushes the string and the economy need not follow, because the central bank can supply liquidity and lower rates but cannot compel households and firms to borrow and spend.

questions.stem: Fiscal policy plays a smaller stabilization role than monetary policy most likely because:

options.A: the fiscal decision-making process is too lengthy for timely adjustments.
options.B: fiscal multipliers are always smaller than monetary multipliers.
options.C: automatic stabilizers already fully offset cyclical swings.

rationales.A: There are two reasons. In all but the most authoritarian regimes, the fiscal decision-making process is too lengthy to make timely adjustments to aggregate spending and taxation aimed at short-term objectives. In addition, frequent changes of a meaningful magnitude would themselves be disruptive. Monetary policy, by contrast, can be adjusted at a scheduled meeting or between meetings.
rationales.B: The relative size of fiscal and monetary multipliers is not the issue, and no general claim that fiscal multipliers are always smaller can be supported. The constraint on discretionary fiscal policy is procedural and structural: the time it takes to legislate a change, and the disruption that frequent sizable changes would cause.
rationales.C: Automatic stabilizers, such as progressive tax regimes and means-based transfer payments, cushion cyclical swings but do not fully offset them, and their existence is not the reason discretionary fiscal policy plays a limited stabilization role. That reason is procedural: the fiscal decision-making process is too lengthy for timely short-term adjustments, and frequent meaningful changes would be disruptive.

questions.stem: A country pursues persistently loose fiscal policy paired with persistently tight monetary policy. The most likely combination of real rates, expected inflation, and nominal rates is:

options.A: Low real rates, high expected inflation, high nominal rates.
options.B: High real rates, low expected inflation, mid nominal rates.
options.C: Low real rates, low expected inflation, low nominal rates.

rationales.A: Low real rates combined with high expected inflation is the signature of the opposite mix, tight fiscal policy paired with loose monetary policy, and that mix produces mid rather than high nominal rates. Loose fiscal policy paired with loose monetary policy is the combination that produces high real rates together with high expected inflation and high nominal rates.
rationales.B: Loose fiscal policy pushes real rates high, because the private sector must save more to absorb the government's borrowing or capital must be attracted from abroad. Tight monetary policy holds expected inflation low. Nominal rates combine the two components, so the high real rate and the low inflation expectation partially offset and the result is a mid nominal rate.
rationales.C: Low real rates together with low expected inflation and low nominal rates is the signature of tight fiscal policy paired with tight monetary policy: light government borrowing leaves real rates low and restrictive monetary policy keeps inflation expectations low, so both components of the nominal rate are low.

questions.curriculum_ref: Section 10 — Exhibit 6, policy mix and rate levels

questions.stem: Monetary policy is subject to long and variable lags. The practical implication for central banks and analysts is most likely that:

options.A: the central bank should wait until inflation has materialized before acting.
options.B: policy changes affect the economy with a fixed, predictable delay.
options.C: the central bank's ability to fine-tune the economy is limited.

rationales.A: Waiting until inflation has fully materialized ignores the lags. By the time such a policy response took effect, conditions would have moved on and the response could exacerbate rather than moderate the cycle. Central banks must act pre-emptively despite forecast uncertainty.
rationales.B: The lags are variable as well as long. Neither their length nor their timing can be treated as a fixed, predictable delay to be built directly into a forecast, which is precisely why fine-tuning the economy is so difficult.
rationales.C: The impact of monetary policy is subject to long and variable lags, as well as to substantial uncertainty. As a result, a central bank's ability to fine-tune the economy is limited, and there is always a risk that policy measures will exacerbate rather than moderate the business cycle. The risk is greatest at the top of the cycle, when the central bank may overestimate the economy's momentum and tighten into a slowdown that is already under way.

questions.curriculum_ref: Analysis of Monetary and Fiscal Policies — long and variable lags

questions.stem: A fiscal automatic stabilizer is most likely illustrated by:

options.A: discretionary tax rate cuts announced quarterly by legislatures.
options.B: progressive tax regimes and means-based transfer payments.
options.C: central bank policy rate adjustments through open market operations.

rationales.A: Discretionary changes are not automatic. They require legislative action, and that process is too slow to serve a stabilization purpose; by the time a quarterly announcement took effect the cyclical position it was aimed at may have passed.
rationales.B: The automatic stabilizers are progressive tax regimes, which imply that the effective tax rate on the private sector is procyclical, rising as the economy expands and falling as it contracts, and means-based transfer payments, which vary inversely with the economy. Both operate without any new decision being taken, and together they help mitigate fluctuations in disposable income for the most vulnerable households.
rationales.C: The policy rate is discretionary monetary policy, set by decision at each meeting, not fiscal automatic stabilization. Automatic stabilizers are features of the tax and transfer system that respond to the cycle without a decision being made.

questions.curriculum_ref: Analysis of Monetary and Fiscal Policies — automatic stabilizers

questions.stem: When short-term policy rates are negative, the baseline risk-free rate used in constructing long-run capital market expectations is most likely:

options.A: zero, regardless of observed rates.
options.B: the long-run equilibrium short-term rate.
options.C: the observed negative short-term rate.

rationales.A: A specific estimation method applies rather than substituting zero. The baseline is the long-run equilibrium short-term rate, which is estimated from the central bank's reaction function and is neither the observed rate nor an arbitrary zero floor.
rationales.B: Long-run capital market expectations typically take the risk-free rate as a baseline. When short-term rates are negative, the long-run equilibrium short-term rate can be used as that baseline instead of the observed negative rate. The equilibrium rate can be estimated using the neutral policy rate (r_neutral) in the Taylor rule, or more generally in the central bank's presumed reaction function, adjusted for a modest spread between policy rates and the default-free rates actually available to investors.
rationales.C: Using the observed negative rate as-is unduly reduces expected returns for risky instruments. Risk premiums are added on top of the baseline, so a negative anchor depresses every long-run risky-asset forecast built from it.

questions.curriculum_ref: Analysis of Monetary and Fiscal Policies — negative rates baseline

drills.reading_name: Capital Market Expectations, Part 1: Framework and Macro Considerations

questions.stem: The slope of the default-free term structure most likely depends primarily on:

options.A: the maturity mix of government debt issuance.
options.B: the current policy rate and the term premium.
options.C: the expected path of short-term rates and a maturity premium.

rationales.A: The maturity mix of government debt issuance may have a temporary effect while the flow is occurring, but it is not one of the two primary drivers of curve slope.
rationales.B: The slope depends on expected future short rates, not on the current policy rate alone. Today's policy rate anchors the very front end of the curve but says nothing by itself about the path markets expect, which is what shapes the rest of the curve.
rationales.C: The slope depends primarily on (1) the expected future path of short-term rates and (2) a risk premium required to compensate for the greater price volatility inherent in longer-maturity bonds. That maturity premium is why the term structure is normally upward sloping.

questions.curriculum_ref: Section 10 — determinants of yield curve slope

questions.stem: An economy is transitioning from initial recovery to early expansion. The most likely pattern for the yield curve at this transition is that:

options.A: short rates and bond yields decline and the curve steepens.
options.B: short rates move up, long yields hold or rise slightly, and the curve flattens.
options.C: short rates peak, bond yields top out, and the curve is flat to inverted.

rationales.A: Declining short rates and bond yields with a steepening curve describe the contraction phase, when the central bank is cutting aggressively and the front end falls faster than the long end. That is the opposite of the move into early expansion.
rationales.B: In early expansion, money market rates move up and bond yields rise, possibly remaining stable at the longest maturities, so the curve flattens. The driver is the central bank withdrawing the stimulus put in place during the recovery, which lifts the front end faster than the long end.
rationales.C: Peaking short rates, topped-out bond yields and a flat-to-inverted curve describe the slowdown phase late in the cycle, after the tightening has largely been delivered, not the transition out of initial recovery.

questions.curriculum_ref: Section 10 — Exhibit 7, rates over the cycle

questions.stem: The 10-year minus 3-month Treasury yield spread has historically been useful for predicting economic growth. This predictive relationship most likely passes the test for a good model because:

options.A: econometric analysis alone confirms it, without theoretical support.
options.B: it has held in every business cycle since 1854.
options.C: a solid economic rationale explains why curve shape should predict growth.

rationales.A: Empirical relationships without an economic rationale are a warning sign of data-mining bias: no story, no future. Econometric fit on its own is precisely what the test for a good model refuses to accept, so it cannot be the reason this relationship passes.
rationales.B: No claim of universal consistency across every cycle is made, and none would be credible. Empirical relationships of this kind vary considerably in strength and in lead time from one cycle to the next.
rationales.C: The empirical link between the shape of the yield curve and subsequent growth passes the test set out for a good model because there is a solid rationale for believing it should be predictive. Expectations of the path of short-term rates are the primary determinant of the curve's shape, so the curve carries information about market participants' views of how the economy will evolve.

questions.curriculum_ref: Section 10 — yield curve as economic predictor

questions.stem: The most likely effect on the yield curve of very large purchases of long-dated bonds by a central bank is:

options.A: no effect, since government bond markets are too liquid to be moved.
options.B: a noticeable effect while buying occurs, unlikely to be sustained afterward.
options.C: a permanent flattening that persists after the purchases end.

rationales.A: A meaningful effect does occur while the flow is in progress. Sufficiently large operations move the curve at the maturities being bought; the question at issue is the durability of that effect, not its existence.
rationales.B: Sufficiently large purchases or sales at different maturities are likely to have a meaningful effect on the curve while they are occurring, but the effect is unlikely to be sustained for long once the buy or sell operation ends. Government bonds are liquid enough that investors move up and down the curve to exploit even small yield differentials, which arbitrages the distortion away.
rationales.C: The flattening is not permanent. The effect is unlikely to be sustained for long after the operation ends, because investors reposition along the curve as soon as the official flow stops and the yield differential it created disappears.

questions.stem: The yield curve slope is countercyclical. Its most likely pattern over the business cycle is:

options.A: inverted at the trough, flattening in expansion, steepening at the peak.
options.B: flat at the trough, steepening in expansion, inverting in contraction.
options.C: steep at the trough, very flat or inverted at the peak, re-steepening in contraction.

rationales.A: This inverts the actual pattern at both ends of the cycle. The curve is steep, not inverted, at the trough, and it is very flat or inverted at the peak rather than steepening there.
rationales.B: The timing is wrong across the cycle. The curve is already steep at the trough rather than flat, it flattens rather than steepens through the expansion, and it re-steepens rather than inverts during the contraction.
rationales.C: The countercyclical pattern runs as follows: the curve tends to be steep at the bottom of the cycle, flattens during the expansion until it is very flat or even inverted at the peak, and re-steepens during the subsequent contraction. This happens because expectations for the path of short-term rates are the primary determinant of the curve's shape, and those expectations shift from easing to tightening and back again as the cycle progresses.

questions.curriculum_ref: The Shape of the Yield Curve and the Business Cycle

questions.stem: A country's government debt-to-GDP ratio is high and rising because of persistent fiscal deficits. The most likely risk this creates is that the central bank will:

options.A: reduce the money supply sharply to impose fiscal discipline.
options.B: be coerced into inflating away the real value of the debt.
options.C: become fully independent of the fiscal authority.

rationales.A: Sharp tightening is what a coerced central bank cannot do. Contracting the money supply would raise real debt service costs and worsen the fiscal arithmetic. The risk runs the other way, toward accommodation that inflates the debt away and steepens the yield curve.
rationales.B: Where government debt is high relative to GDP and rising because of large deficits, there is a risk the central bank is coerced into inflating away the real value of the debt with accommodative monetary policy. This dynamic is almost certain to steepen the yield curve, and if realized it is likely to lead to an inflationary spiral: higher inflation leads to higher nominal rates, which accelerates debt accumulation, which in turn calls for still more accommodation.
rationales.C: The warning runs the opposite way. Heavy debt loads create political pressure on rate policy that erodes central bank independence rather than reinforcing it.

questions.curriculum_ref: The Monetary and Fiscal Policy Mix — politicization risk

questions.stem: Shifts in the relative supply of government bonds across maturities generally have only transient effects on the yield curve. The exception most likely arises at:

options.A: the short end, where bill issuance is largest relative to trading demand.
options.B: intermediate maturities, where trading volume is heaviest.
options.C: very long maturities, where liability-driven buyers have few substitutes.

rationales.A: The short end is anchored by the policy rate and is extremely liquid, so shifts in bill supply do not create sustained yield distortions however large the issuance is relative to trading demand.
rationales.B: Intermediate maturities are highly liquid, and investors readily move along the curve to exploit even small yield differentials, so supply effects there dissipate once the buying or selling operation ends. Heavy trading volume is a reason supply shifts are absorbed, not a reason they persist.
rationales.C: At very long maturities, dedicated buyers with liability-driven mandates, pension funds in particular, have few substitutes for the longest bonds. Shifts in relative supply in that segment can therefore exert sustained pressure on yields, unlike the transient effects seen elsewhere on the curve.

questions.curriculum_ref: The Monetary and Fiscal Policy Mix — maturity supply effects

drills.los_text: identify and interpret macroeconomic, interest rate, and exchange rate linkages between economies
drills.reading_name: Capital Market Expectations, Part 1: Framework and Macro Considerations

questions.stem: Of the following combinations of policy goals, the one a country is least likely to be able to pursue simultaneously is:

options.A: free trade, a floating exchange rate, and low inflation.
options.B: a balanced current account, a stable currency, and price stability.
options.C: unrestricted capital flows, a fixed exchange rate, and independent monetary policy.

rationales.A: These three goals are not identified as mutually exclusive. A floating exchange rate is in fact what frees monetary policy to target low inflation, and free trade is compatible with both, so this combination is not the impossible trinity.
rationales.B: This is not the trinity, and these three goals are not incompatible. A country can run a balanced current account alongside a stable currency and price stability.
rationales.C: The impossible trinity holds that a country cannot simultaneously (i) allow unrestricted capital flows, (ii) maintain a fixed exchange rate, and (iii) pursue an independent monetary policy. Attempting all three fails because any attempt to set domestic rates away from the level consistent with the peg induces offsetting capital flows that undo the monetary policy.

questions.stem: Under the national income identity, the most likely implication of a country running a current account deficit is that:

options.A: domestic saving exceeds domestic investment plus the government surplus.
options.B: a capital account surplus funds spending in excess of saving plus taxes.
options.C: net exports are zero on average over the business cycle.

rationales.A: Saving in excess of investment plus the government surplus is the current account surplus condition, the mirror image of a deficit. Since (X − M) = (S − I) + (T − G), a deficit requires the right-hand side to be negative, meaning domestic saving falls short of investment plus the government balance.
rationales.B: The identity is (X − M) = (S − I) + (T − G). A current account deficit implies (S − I) + (T − G) is negative, and a surplus on the capital account is how a nation funds an excess of investment and government spending over domestic saving plus taxes.
rationales.C: The identity applies at every point in time, not only when averaged over the business cycle. A current account deficit means net exports are negative now, not zero on average.

questions.stem: Empirical evidence indicates overwhelmingly that purchasing power parity (PPP) does not hold over relevant investment horizons. For a domestic investor considering non-domestic bonds, the most likely implication is that:

options.A: The investor's real return will differ from the non-domestic real interest rate.
options.B: PPP-based currency forecasts should replace the interest rate parity condition.
options.C: Real interest rate differentials are exploitable arbitrage opportunities.

rationales.A: Unless PPP holds over the investor's horizon, the real return earned in her own currency will not equal the non-domestic real interest rate, even if non-domestic interest rates remain unchanged. The realized real return combines the foreign nominal return with the exchange rate movement and the investor's own domestic inflation. Only if relative inflation rates and the spot exchange rate move together, which is the PPP condition, do those two adjustments cancel and leave the foreign real rate intact. Because PPP fails over investment horizons, they do not cancel, and the investor bears a real currency effect on top of the foreign real rate.
rationales.B: PPP-based currency forecasts are not a substitute for interest rate parity. Covered interest rate parity is an arbitrage relationship that must hold among spot rates, forward rates and nominal interest rates, whereas PPP is a weak long-run equilibrium tendency that the empirical evidence shows failing at the horizons investors actually care about. Replacing the condition that does hold with the one that does not runs in the wrong direction.
rationales.C: The implication runs the other way. Because PPP does not hold over the relevant horizon, one cannot rely on the simplistic notion that real interest rate differentials represent exploitable opportunities. Capturing a higher foreign real rate requires the exchange rate to adjust in line with relative inflation, and that adjustment is exactly what the evidence says does not reliably occur, so the differential carries unhedged real currency risk rather than an arbitrage profit.

questions.curriculum_ref: Section 11 — PPP and real interest rate differentials

questions.stem: Two eurozone countries — Germany and a peripheral country — trade in the same currency. When the market perceives an imminent risk that the peripheral country will exit the euro, the most likely effect on the peripheral country's yield curve is that:

options.A: Spreads over Germany narrow across the curve.
options.B: Spreads over Germany widen across the curve, most at the shortest maturities, and the curve inverts.
options.C: Spreads over Germany widen only at the longest maturities.

rationales.A: Spreads widen rather than narrow in this scenario. Perceived redenomination or devaluation risk drives capital out of the peripheral country and toward the safer market, so peripheral yields rise relative to German yields and spreads over Germany increase. A narrowing would imply capital moving toward the country whose currency risk has just increased.
rationales.B: When the market perceives an imminent threat of devaluation or exit, spreads widen throughout the curve, but especially at the shortest maturities, and the curve will almost certainly invert. The reason is that in the event of devaluation, yields decline sharply as the currency risk premium collapses, generating larger capital gains on longer-term bonds and so mitigating more of the currency loss. Investors therefore demand less compensation per year of exposure at the long end than at the short end, where there is almost no price cushion against an immediate devaluation. The short-maturity spread consequently widens furthest and the curve inverts.
rationales.C: The widening is concentrated at the short end, not the long end. Longer-term bonds offer a cushion: if the currency is devalued, the collapse in the currency risk premium produces a large price gain on long duration that offsets much of the currency loss, so investors require relatively less spread there. Short-dated bonds have no such cushion, so their spreads widen most and the curve inverts rather than steepening on rising term premia.

questions.stem: The current account in a country's balance of payments is best described as reflecting:

options.A: Net exports of goods only.
options.B: Net exports of goods and services, net investment income, and unilateral transfers.
options.C: Net investment flows for direct investment and portfolio investment.

rationales.A: The current account is broader than merchandise trade. It covers net exports of goods and services, net investment income flows and unilateral transfers, so excluding services and transfers understates it. Traded services and remittances are frequently large components of a country's current account balance.
rationales.B: The current account reflects net exports of goods and services, net investment income flows (income earned on assets held abroad net of income paid to foreign holders of domestic assets) and unilateral transfers such as remittances and foreign aid. By construction it is the mirror image of the capital and financial accounts: a current account surplus must be matched by a capital account deficit, and vice versa, because a country that sells more than it buys must be acquiring claims on the rest of the world.
rationales.C: Net investment flows for foreign direct investment and portfolio investment describe the capital and financial accounts, not the current account. Those accounts record cross-border transactions in productive and financial assets, whereas the current account records flows of goods, services, investment income and transfers.

questions.stem: The capital account, taken to include the financial account, is best described as reflecting:

options.A: Net exports of goods and services and unilateral transfers.
options.B: Net investment flows for direct investment and portfolio investment.
options.C: Central bank reserve transactions only.

rationales.A: Net exports of goods and services together with unilateral transfers describe the current account, not the capital account. These are flows of output and income rather than flows of claims on assets.
rationales.B: The capital account, taken here to include what is formally the financial account, reflects net investment flows: foreign direct investment, meaning the purchase and sale of productive assets across borders, and portfolio investment flows, meaning transactions in financial assets. By construction a current account surplus must be matched by a capital account deficit, or vice versa, since the two accounts are opposite sides of the same set of cross-border transactions.
rationales.C: Central bank reserve transactions are one narrow subcategory of official flows. The capital and financial accounts are far broader, encompassing foreign direct investment in productive assets and portfolio investment in financial assets by private as well as official participants.

questions.stem: Although real interest rates around the world need not be equal, they tend to move together. This is most likely because:

options.A: Global saving must always equal global investment.
options.B: Purchasing power parity holds tightly over investment horizons.
options.C: Central banks coordinate real rate targets internationally.

rationales.A: Real interest rates must ultimately be consistent with the real saving and investment decisions that drive economic growth and the productivity of capital. There is a global market in which capital flows to where it is expected to be most productive, and although real rates need not be equal across countries, they are linked by the requirement that global savings must always equal global investment. That linkage is why they tend to move together. Persistently low real rates after the global financial crisis are widely attributed to high global saving, primarily in Asia, combined with low capital investment in developed markets.
rationales.B: Purchasing power parity does not hold over relevant investment horizons; the empirical evidence against it is overwhelming. Co-movement in real rates therefore cannot be attributed to a tight PPP link between relative prices and exchange rates.
rationales.C: Co-movement does not depend on explicit international coordination of real rate targets. Central banks set policy against domestic mandates; the linkage arises from the global saving and investment balance and from the mobility of capital toward its most productive use, not from any coordination agreement.
